items.title: Omar Abdihamid Shares Insights on the Future of Oncology at KESHO 2026
items.description: Omar Abdihamid Shares Insights on the Future of Oncology at KESHO 2026 / cancer care, Cancer research, Kenya, Kenya Society of Haematology and Oncology,
content: Omar Abdihamid , Clinical Oncologist at Shabaha Cancer Centre and Clinical Oncology Specialist at Garissa Regional Cancer Centre, shared on LinkedIn :
“Honoured to be part of the 9th Kenya Society of Haematology and Oncology (KESHO) KICC Conference , happening here in Mombasa, Kenya.
It was a privilege to contribute as a speaker and a scientific committe member and engage with colleagues from across region and beyond on the issues shaping the future of cancer care.

Conferences like KICC are more than just scientific meetings – they are spaces where we exchange ideas, challenge conventional thinking, build collaborations, and most importantly, ask how we can translate evidence into better outcomes for our patients.
As oncologists, our responsibility goes beyond knowing the latest evidence. We must also ask : How do we make that evidence work in the realities of our health systems and for the patients we serve?
Grateful for the opportunity to learn, share, and connect with so many inspiring colleagues.
KESHO (Kenya Society of Haematology and Oncology) is a professional organization dedicated to improving cancer and blood disorder care in Kenya through education, research and collaboration.

Its 9th Kenya International Cancer Conference (KICC 2026) took place on November 19–21 in Mombasa, bringing together oncologists, researchers and other healthcare professionals from across the region and beyond.

The conference focused on improving access to cancer care, advancing research, sharing clinical knowledge and strengthening healthcare systems, with an emphasis on turning scientific evidence into better outcomes for patients.

items.title: Matiang’i dismisses two-camp opposition claims
items.description: Matiang’i has dismissed claims of rival camps within the opposition, insisting there is only one united team preparing to challenge President William Ruto in 2027.
content: NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 22 – Jubilee Party presidential hopeful Fred Matiang’i has dismissed claims of competing political camps within the opposition, insisting that the movement is united and will field one candidate against President William Ruto in the 2027 General Election.

Matiang’i, who is positioning himself for the opposition’s presidential ticket, said leaders should not be distracted by claims of internal divisions but instead focus on consolidating their political bases and building a united front ahead of the polls.

Speaking during a church service attended by Narc Kenya leader Martha Karua and Kiharu MP Ndindi Nyoro, Matiang’i explained his association with the two leaders, saying they shared a common approach to leadership and a desire to provide solutions to Kenya’s challenges.
He described Karua as a leader he admired for her straightforwardness and firm approach to issues, adding that their shared values informed their political relationship.

“First of all, my elder sister Mother Karua is someone I always look up to because we have a lot of things in common. I like her a lot because she is also no-nonsense. She’s also focused on the things we do; that’s why I keep her company,” Matiang’i said.

items.title: Kalonzo takes his 2027 campaign to the pews and the people of Mwala
items.description: Wiper leader Kalonzo Musyoka visited Mwala Constituency in Machakos County at the weekend, rallying residents and attending church as his 2027 presidential campaign intensifies.
content: The Wiper leader’s Machakos County tour blends faith, constitutional messaging, and grassroots mobilisation as the race for State House moves into its most consequential phase.

Wiper Party leader Kalonzo Musyoka carried his 2027 presidential campaign into Machakos County at the weekend, addressing residents of Mwala Constituency and attending Sunday worship at AIC Mbaikini in Wamunyu Ward in a visit that combined grassroots political outreach with a carefully framed constitutional message.

The former Vice-President received a warm reception in Wamunyu, where he addressed residents and laid out the ideological foundation on which he intends to contest the August 2027 General Election. His message was pointed and deliberate. “The people of Mwala have made a commitment to stand for a better Kenya — a nation founded on constitutionalism, the rule of law, justice and respect for the rights and freedoms of every citizen,” Kalonzo told the gathering. “We want a nation where the constitution is supreme, where institutions serve the people, where justice is accessible to all, and where no Kenyan is above the law.”

The declaration — “It is liberation time” — that closed his public address served as both a campaign slogan and a signal of intent. For Kalonzo, who has contested the presidency three times and watched victory slip away on each occasion, the framing of 2027 as a moment of constitutional reckoning rather than a simple electoral contest reflects a strategic repositioning. He is not merely running against a candidate; he is running against what his campaign characterises as institutional decay and constitutional subversion.

The Sunday church service added a different but complementary dimension to the visit. Joining worshippers at AIC Mbaikini, Kalonzo used the occasion to anchor his political mission in faith and communal responsibility. “Our faith reminds us that, in every season, we must seek God’s wisdom and remain steadfast in our duty to one another,” he said. “Let us continue to pray for our families, our communities and our country, asking God to guide our leaders and grant Kenya peace, unity and a just future.” He drew on Psalm 33:12 — “Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord, the people he chose for his inheritance” — to underscore his message.

The visit was not a solo endeavour. Kalonzo was accompanied by a delegation that underlined the breadth of support he is assembling in the region. Democratic Party leader Justin Muturi, Wiper Party Foundation National Chairman Jamleck Kamau, Machakos Deputy Governor Francis Mwangangi, Machakos Women Representative Joyce Kamene, Machakos Senator Agnes Kavindu, Members of Parliament Julius Mawathe and Makali Mulu, and Wiper Party Foundation spokesperson Ndegwa Njiru were all present — a show of force that the Wiper leader’s campaign will hope translates into organised electoral infrastructure as the race intensifies.

The political significance of Machakos County in the 2027 contest cannot be overstated. The Ukambani region — comprising Machakos, Kitui, and Makueni counties — delivered a substantial bloc of votes for Kalonzo in previous elections, and consolidating that base while reaching beyond it remains central to any realistic path to State House. A weekend that moves between a public rally and a church service in a single constituency reflects the rhythm of a campaign that understands the terrain: in Ukambani, as in much of rural Kenya, political persuasion happens as much in places of worship and community gatherings as it does on the rally ground.

The timing of the Mwala visit is also instructive. Kenya’s political calendar is accelerating. With the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission under sustained opposition pressure over electoral preparedness, voter registration timelines, and results transmission architecture, the window for meaningful pre-campaign positioning is narrowing. Opposition leaders who fail to build visible, organised grassroots structures in this period risk arriving at the campaign season with name recognition but without the organisational machinery that converts votes into a result.

Kalonzo’s constitutional framing — supremacy of law, independent institutions, justice for all — is calibrated to appeal beyond his traditional Ukambani base to the reform-minded urban and middle-class voters who swung behind the Gen Z protest movement in 2024 and have remained politically restless since. Whether that appeal translates into a broadened coalition or remains a regional consolidation exercise will be one of the defining questions of the 2027 opposition contest.

The Wiper leader goes into 2027 as a seasoned, battle-tested political figure who understands both the possibilities and the cruelties of Kenyan presidential politics. He has been this close before — close enough to know how little separates ambition from arrival. This time, he is making the case not simply that he deserves the presidency, but that Kenya’s democratic institutions demand the kind of leadership he represents.

Whether Kenyans agree will be settled in August. For now, Kalonzo is in the constituency, in the church, and in the conversation — and that, in the long march to State House, is exactly where a candidate needs to be.

items.title: Wetangula declares 2032 presidential bid after Ruto’s second term
items.description: National Assembly Speaker Moses Wetangula has announced his 2032 presidential bid, citing decades of experience and backing President Ruto's 2027 re-election first.
content: The National Assembly Speaker says decades of legislative and administrative experience make him the right successor to President William Ruto.

National Assembly Speaker Moses Wetangula has declared his intention to contest the presidency in 2032, announcing his ambition publicly on Sunday and urging Western Kenya to unite behind him in pursuit of a seat the region has long coveted.

Wetangula, who entered Parliament in 1992 and has served across successive administrations in senior legislative and cabinet roles, argued that his record positions him as the natural successor to President William Ruto upon completion of a second term. “I have the energy, experience and commitment required to serve this country, build on the progress President Ruto has initiated and safeguard the gains made under his leadership,” he said.

The Speaker grounded his argument in Kenya’s presidential history, noting that every occupant of State House since independence has arrived there through sustained political experience rather than overnight ambition. He used that logic to dismiss first-time Members of Parliament entertaining 2027 presidential ambitions, telling a rally at Jepkoyayi Grounds in Hamisi Constituency, Vihiga County: “There is no miracle in winning the presidency in Kenya. Kenyans have always put their trust in experienced politicians.”
Wetangula stopped short of distancing himself from the current administration, explicitly backing Ruto’s 2027 re-election before staking his own claim for what comes after.
For Western Kenya, the declaration is both a rallying call and a long-range political promise — one the region will now watch Wetangula work to keep.

items.title: Kenya 2027: Political realignments reshaping the road to State House
items.description: Kenya's 2027 election race intensifies as NLP quits Azimio, opposition leaders walk out of IEBC talks, and presidential ambitions multiply across the political divide.
content: As coalitions fracture, opposition leaders walk out of IEBC talks, and a potential third force takes shape around Karua, Matiang’i, and Ndindi Nyoro, Kenya’s path to August 2027 is growing more complicated by the week.

Kenya’s political landscape is shifting rapidly ahead of the August 2027 General Election, with coalition defections, opposition disagreements, competing presidential ambitions, and the emergence of a potential third-force political formation combining to reshape a contest that once appeared straightforward into something considerably more unpredictable.

The latest signal of that turbulence came on November 21, when the National Liberal Party, led by Dr August Muli, announced its immediate withdrawal from the Azimio la Umoja One Kenya Coalition. The decision, taken after consultations with the party’s National Executive Council, county chairpersons, delegates, and grassroots members, was framed not as hostility toward former partners but as a matter of principle. The party stated that the coalition no longer reflected its values, vision, or political aspirations — and that it intended to chart its own course, including unveiling a presidential candidate at a forthcoming National Delegates Convention and fielding candidates across all elective positions, from governor to member of county assembly.

The departure is not an isolated event. It is the latest episode in a broader fragmentation of opposition politics raising legitimate questions about whether Kenya’s anti-government forces can consolidate around a credible alternative before the campaign period begins in earnest.

Two days earlier, on November 19, those questions grew sharper still. Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua, Wiper Party leader Kalonzo Musyoka, Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna, former Chief Justice David Maraga, and other senior opposition figures walked out of a consultative meeting with the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission, accusing the electoral body of failing to adequately address their concerns about the management of the upcoming election.

Their demands were substantive: regular structured consultations with the IEBC, transparency in the transmission of presidential results, an independent audit of the voter register, and greater accountability in the oversight of election technology. These are not fringe concerns. They go to the heart of electoral credibility — and their public articulation reflects a deep anxiety within the opposition about the institutional conditions under which the 2027 contest will be conducted.

The IEBC responded by arguing that the walkout denied participants the very opportunity for dialogue they were demanding. It is a defensible point, but it does not resolve the underlying tension. Electoral commissions earn trust through demonstrated impartiality and transparent communication, not through procedural arguments about meeting etiquette. The commission must do more than defend its process; it must visibly strengthen it.

Notably, dissatisfaction with the consultation process is not confined to the opposition. United Democratic Alliance chairperson Cecily Mbarire raised concerns about the alleged harassment of government-aligned delegates during the same November 19 engagement and warned of a possible boycott of future meetings if the situation remained unaddressed. When parties across the political spectrum are questioning the conduct of electoral consultations, the IEBC faces a credibility challenge that transcends partisan politics.

Hovering over all of this, with growing momentum, is the prospect of a third political force — one that could redraw the entire electoral map if it coheres into a formal coalition. Martha Karua, leader of the People’s Liberation Party, former Interior Cabinet Secretary Fred Matiang’i, and Kiharu Member of Parliament Ndindi Nyoro are among the figures whose names are increasingly circulating in connection with an alternative political platform that sits outside both the government’s UDA machinery and the established Azimio framework. What unites them is a combination of Mount Kenya political capital, credibility with reform-minded voters, and a shared distance from the current administration.

The potential addition of Siaya Governor James Orengo — one of Kenya’s most seasoned constitutional lawyers and a figure with deep roots in opposition politics — would add further intellectual and political heft to such a formation. Orengo’s possible involvement signals that the third-force conversation is no longer confined to whisper networks; it is being taken seriously by figures with the institutional standing to make it real.

The implications are significant. A credible third force drawing support from Mount Kenya, the Coast, Western Kenya, and reform constituencies could complicate the electoral mathematics for both President William Ruto and the existing opposition blocs. It could also offer voters an alternative to what many perceive as a binary choice between the status quo and a fragmented opposition — a choice that has historically suppressed turnout among disenchanted urban and middle-class voters.

The deeper question hovering over all of this is whether Kenya’s opposition, in its various configurations, can construct coherent political strategies in time to mount credible challenges. Coalition politics in Kenya has historically turned on the consolidation of presidential candidacies — parties that fragment their support across multiple candidates have consistently underperformed at the ballot. The current landscape, with several prominent figures openly positioning for the presidency across multiple formations, risks repeating that pattern.

History offers a sobering lesson. Kenya’s electoral coalitions have too often been built around tactical convenience rather than shared policy commitments, cohering around a candidate and dissolving when the mathematics of political negotiation become uncomfortable. If any opposition grouping is to avoid that fate in 2027, it needs not just a coalition agreement but a compelling policy platform — one that speaks directly to the economic realities confronting ordinary Kenyans.

Those realities are pressing. Unemployment remains stubbornly high. The cost of living continues to squeeze household budgets. Public services are stretched. Educational financing remains a source of acute anxiety for families across the country. Young Kenyans — the demographic that proved decisive in recent political cycles — are not simply watching political realignments with detached interest. They are evaluating them against a standard of practical relevance: what will any of this actually do for my life?

Political parties competing for State House in 2027 would do well to internalise that question. The contest cannot be reduced to a competition over personalities, defections, and the allocation of coalition positions. Voters deserve detailed, costed, credible policy commitments — on employment, healthcare, agriculture, education, and the broader direction of the economy. A coalition’s value should be measured not by the prominence of the names on its platform but by the quality of what it is promising to do with power.

Kenya’s road to State House will ultimately be decided not in the boardrooms where coalition deals are struck, but at the polling station — by millions of citizens evaluating candidates against their own lived experience. The withdrawal of the National Liberal Party from Azimio, the IEBC walkout, the proliferating presidential ambitions, and the quiet assembly of a third-force formation around Karua, Matiang’i, Ndindi Nyoro, and potentially Orengo are all symptoms of a political system in motion. Whether that motion produces democratic renewal or electoral confusion will depend on choices that political leaders must make in the months immediately ahead.

The responsibility is clear. Build credible institutions. Present honest platforms. Respect the electorate. Kenyans are not spectators in a game played by powerful individuals. They are the point of the exercise — and in August 2027, they will have the final word.

items.title: The Standard questions Ruto’s claims and the meaning of progress
items.description: The Standard’s two critiques question both the evidence behind the President’s claims and whether headline achievements reflect rights, security and household costs.
content: The Standard’s two critiques question both the evidence behind the President’s claims and whether headline achievements reflect rights, security and household costs.

President William Ruto’s State of the Nation address on November 18 left two questions in The Standard’s coverage: whether the figures behind the government’s claims can be checked, and whether those claims describe progress in people’s lives.

The Standard’s two opinion pieces approach the address differently. One takes on the arithmetic. The other challenges the idea that a list of achievements, even if accurate, is enough to show that the country is moving in the right direction. Both say the account presented by the President did not adequately reflect Kenyans’ experience.

The more detailed critique calls for Parliament to revisit a claim Ruto made in November 2025 that the 2024 maize harvest was 67 million bags . The Standard says Citizen TV compared that figure with a Kenya National Bureau of Statistics total of 44.7 million, leaving a gap of 22.3 million bags. The article asks whether the numbers used comparable methods and calls on the Agriculture Cabinet Secretary to explain the source and measurement. The supplied coverage does not provide a government response or resolve the discrepancy.

The jobs figures also get a closer reading. KNBS recorded 822,100 additional jobs in 2025 , excluding small-scale agriculture; 716,800, or 87.2 per cent, were informal. The Standard argues that counting new work is not the same as showing it is secure or well paid. That is an argument about the quality of employment, not a dispute over the reported totals.

On household finances, the article sets TIFA survey results against official inflation figures. In the June 2026 survey, 65 per cent said their circumstances had worsened since the 2022 election and 12 per cent said they had improved. KNBS reported October annual inflation of 7.3 per cent , with food and non-alcoholic beverages up 10.2 per cent and transport up 17.1 per cent. The piece uses those figures to explain why national claims of progress may feel distant from daily costs.

The first article also points to the Treasury’s projected Sh1.116 trillion deficit for 2026/27, asking the government to show what borrowing has achieved. It questions the appointment of former Meru governor Kiraitu Murungi to chair the National Oil Corporation board, asking what expertise was required and who else was considered. On civil liberties, it cites a 2024 court finding that the acting police chief was in contempt after repeatedly failing to appear over three men allegedly abducted by police, and says the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights documented further complaints about disappearances and excessive force around protests in 2026. The article ends mid-sentence, so its final point is unavailable.

The second piece is broader and less tied to individual figures. It says Ruto presented a Kenya of “remarkable achievement and rapid transformation”, then asks what progress means if it is not judged by whether people have rights, security and the chance to live with dignity. It invokes Article 132(1)(c) of the Constitution, but the supplied text ends before explaining the article’s full argument.

The two accounts agree on the central criticism but do not provide a full record of the President’s address or a response from State House. The harvest gap, the government’s evidence for its claims, and the outcomes of the named policy and appointment decisions remain untested in the material provided. The coverage is also thin: only The Standard is represented here, through two opinion pieces, so it cannot establish how other outlets assessed the address. items.title: Sifuna opens Linda Mwananchi Movement’s first US office
items.description: The Hackettstown office anchors a US tour with meetings planned in six states, but the reports offer no attendance or membership figures.
content: The Hackettstown office anchors a US tour with meetings planned in six states, but the reports offer no attendance or membership figures.

Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna has opened the Linda Mwananchi Movement’s first international office in Hackettstown, New Jersey, giving the group a formal base for its US diaspora activities ahead of the 2027 General Election.

The opening took place on Saturday, November 21 , as Sifuna led a delegation on a tour of the United States. The movement announced the start of its activities in a message on X. Sifuna said the group was “beginning work officially” and opening its first international office.

People Daily’s two reports trace the shift from plan to event: its Saturday article said the office was due to open at noon; a report published Sunday said it had opened. The coverage describes this as the movement’s first formal international office, but does not give the address beyond Hackettstown or identify who will run it.

The office opening is part of a wider programme of meetings with Kenyans living in the US. Sifuna released the itinerary on November 17 , with stops planned in Pennsylvania, Maryland, Washington DC, Texas, Washington State and California.

The schedule includes town halls, church services, dinners with business communities and meetings with diaspora groups. The next listed engagement after New Jersey was a church service and town hall in Allentown, Pennsylvania, on Sunday, November 22. The delegation was also due to meet communities in Maryland and Washington DC before travelling to Dallas and Houston.

Further activities were planned for Seattle and California, with the tour expected to end with a dinner in Silicon Valley on December 7 . Sifuna acknowledged that the delegation would not reach every city or state and told Kenyans in the US to meet the team where they could.

People Daily presents the office as a base for coordinating diaspora engagement and extending the movement’s organisation beyond Kenya. The stated purpose of the tour is to hear concerns and present the movement’s political agenda. The reports do not describe specific policy proposals or say what the office’s day-to-day operations will involve.

Both accounts connect the opening to political organising ahead of the 2027 election. They describe the office and tour as ways to build relationships with Kenyans abroad, but neither provides evidence of how many people attended the opening or the planned events, nor any indication of the movement’s level of support among diaspora communities.

There is also little independent detail in the coverage: both reports are from the same outlet and rely on the movement’s announcement and Sifuna’s itinerary. The development has had limited outlet coverage in the reports provided, so its wider reception cannot be assessed here.

The open question is whether a US office and a run of diaspora meetings will lead to lasting organisation or political support, either among Kenyans abroad or at home. The reports do not give membership figures, funding details or a measure of what success would look like for the initiative.

items.title: Konza Technopolis Gets Customs Clearance Status to Ease Trade and Attract Investors
items.description: Konza Technopolis has been designated a Customs Area and allocated a customs code by the Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA), paving the way for faster movement of goods and simplified customs procedures for
content: Konza Technopolis has been designated a Customs Area and allocated a customs code by the Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA), paving the way for faster movement of goods and simplified customs procedures for businesses operating within the smart city.

The designation marks a major step towards making Konza’s Special Economic Zone (SEZ) fully operational, particularly for companies involved in manufacturing, technology development and other businesses that depend on importing and exporting goods.
The development is expected to reduce customs-related delays and improve the ease of doing business, making Konza more attractive to local and international investors.
Technopolis Development Authority Chief Executive Officer John Paul Okwiri said the new status addresses a key requirement for businesses seeking to establish operations within the zone.

“The gazettement of Konza Technopolis as a Customs Area and the allocation of a customs code is a significant step towards making our Special Economic Zone fully operational. It will facilitate the movement of goods, simplify customs processes and create a more enabling environment for investors,” said Okwiri.
Konza Technopolis was gazetted as a Special Economic Zone in July 2019 as part of Kenya’s efforts to attract investment in technology, innovation and industrial development.
The latest approval strengthens the regulatory framework needed to support businesses operating within the smart city and advances Kenya’s ambition to become a knowledge-based economy.

items.title: Kenya firms lose KSh95.5B yearly to workplace harassment, CEOs told
items.description: Kenya's private sector loses KSh95.5B annually to workplace harassment, a World Bank-convened CEO roundtable in Nairobi heard on Thursday, citing a 2025 IFC study.
content: A World Bank-convened roundtable in Nairobi has put the staggering cost of gender-based violence and harassment squarely on the boardroom agenda — and the numbers demand a response.

Kenya’s private sector is haemorrhaging KSh95.5 billion every year to gender-based violence and harassment in the workplace — and the executives who can stop it were in the same room on Thursday to hear exactly what it is costing them.

Business leaders gathered in Nairobi for a CEO Roundtable on Advancing Inclusive Workplaces, convened jointly by the World Bank Group, the Federation of Kenya Employers, and the Kenya Private Sector Alliance. The forum brought together senior corporate decision-makers to confront a crisis hiding in plain sight: workplace harassment that destroys productivity, drives away talent, and drains company resources on a scale that few boardrooms have fully reckoned with.

The figures are stark. A 2025 study by the International Finance Corporation — the World Bank Group’s private sector arm — found that gender-based violence and harassment costs Kenya’s private sector an estimated KSh67B in lost productivity and a further KSh28.5B in human resource expenses annually. The study, which examined 26 companies, found that 33.2 per cent of employees had experienced harassment, while a staggering 86 per cent of incidents went unreported. Those affected lost an average of 24.3 working days per year — nearly a month of productive output, quietly disappearing from company ledgers.

Gillian Rogers, IFC’s Principal Country Officer for Kenya, opened the roundtable by framing workplace inclusion not as a social obligation but as an economic imperative. “Together, we can build workplaces where women enter, stay, progress, and lead — where companies can draw on the full strength of their talent, and where inclusion translates into stronger people, stronger businesses, and a more competitive Kenyan economy,” she said.

The discussions ranged across the structural barriers that keep women from advancing in Kenya’s corporate sector. Women currently hold approximately 40 per cent of entry-level private sector roles, a figure that falls to 28 per cent at the C-suite level and drops further to just 14 per cent among chief executive officers. That narrowing pipeline is not accidental. It is the cumulative effect of harassment, unequal promotion practices, inadequate parental support, and institutional cultures that reward conformity over capability.

Childcare emerged as a particularly significant factor. Women in sub-Saharan Africa carry two to three times more unpaid care work than men, a burden that consistently limits career progression and forces women to make choices between professional advancement and family responsibility. IFC evidence presented at the roundtable demonstrates that employer-supported childcare reduces absenteeism and measurably improves productivity — a finding that reframes childcare not as a welfare provision but as a sound business investment.

Jacqueline Mugo, Executive Director and Chief Executive Officer of the Federation of Kenya Employers, was direct about the corporate cost of inaction. “Employers have a responsibility to create workplaces where employees feel safe, are treated fairly and have opportunities to grow. When businesses lose experienced workers because of harassment, unfair practices or inadequate support, they also lose valuable skills and productivity,” she said.

The business case for gender diversity in leadership was reinforced by international evidence shared at the roundtable. Companies with gender-diverse executive teams are 25 per cent more likely to outperform financially, while organisations with diverse management structures report 19 per cent higher innovation revenue. The correlation between inclusion and commercial performance is no longer a matter of debate — it is documented and consistent.

Carole Kariuki, Chief Executive Officer of the Kenya Private Sector Alliance, called on company leaders to do more than invest in women at entry level. “Businesses are investing in developing talented women, but too few are progressing into senior leadership. We need CEOs to take greater responsibility for removing these barriers, strengthening promotion pathways and ensuring that gender equality becomes part of how businesses measure performance and growth,” she said.

The World Bank Group has urged Kenyan companies to adopt EDGE certification — an internationally recognised standard for assessing gender equality across pay equity, leadership representation, and career progression — as a mechanism for holding organisations accountable and tracking measurable progress.

For Kenya’s private sector, the message from Thursday’s roundtable was unambiguous: workplace inclusion is not a corporate social responsibility line item. It is a financial liability when ignored, and a competitive advantage when embraced. The KSh95.5B annual cost of getting it wrong is no longer a figure that any responsible board can afford to overlook.

items.title: Visa appoints Esther Waititu as Head of Southern & Eastern Africa
items.description: Visa has announced the appointment of Esther Waititu as Senior Vice President and Group Country Manager for Southern & Eastern Africa. Based in Johannesburg, Esther will lead Visa's presence across 24 markets
content: Visa has announced the appointment of Esther Waititu as Senior Vice President and Group Country Manager for Southern & Eastern Africa.

Based in Johannesburg, Esther will lead Visa’s presence across 24 markets in Southern and Eastern Africa, working with clients, partners, governments and Visa teams across the region to advance digital payments and advance the industry ecosystem. Esther joins Visa with more than two decades of experience across financial services and payments in Africa, with leadership experience spanning mobile money, corporate banking and retail banking.

Most recently, Esther served as Chief Financial Services Officer at Safaricom, where she led M-PESA’s business across payments, credit, savings, investments and insurance. She previously served as Director of Corporate Banking at KCB Bank Group and spent a decade in senior roles at Standard Bank Group, Standard Chartered and Commercial Bank of Africa, now NCBA.

“Southern and Eastern Africa is home to some of the world’s most dynamic and rapidly growing payments markets, and the opportunities ahead are significant. Esther brings deep industry expertise, a strong understanding of the region and a proven ability to build businesses and partnerships at scale. I am delighted to welcome her to Visa and look forward to working with her as we continue to grow our business and deepen our partnerships across the region,” said Tareq Muhmood, Regional President Visa CEMEA,

“I am excited to join Visa at an important moment for digital commerce across Africa. Southern and Eastern Africa is an incredibly diverse region, with enormous potential to expand access, enable businesses and create new ways for consumers and communities to participate in the digital economy. I look forward to working with Visa’s teams, clients and partners across the region to build on the strong foundations already in place and unlock the next phase of growth,” said Esther Waititu.

items.title: Kenya’s AI cancer ambitions face test as doctors warns of gaps in patient care
items.description: Kenya's push to use artificial intelligence in cancer diagnosis could be undermined by fragmented patient records, weak referral systems and unequal access to specialist treatment, medical experts have warned. Speaking at the
content: Kenya’s push to use artificial intelligence in cancer diagnosis could be undermined by fragmented patient records, weak referral systems and unequal access to specialist treatment, medical experts have warned.

Speaking at the 9th Kenya International Cancer Conference in Mombasa over the weekend, veteran physician Prof. Joseph Aluoch said AI could help doctors detect cancer earlier and improve treatment decisions, but its effectiveness would depend on hospitals being able to share accurate patient information.
The warning comes as the country grapples with an estimated 35,867 new cancer cases and nearly 23,000 deaths annually, according to figures cited from the Global Cancer Observatory.
Prof. Aluoch said disconnected hospital information systems could limit the benefits of AI, particularly for patients who seek diagnosis and treatment at different facilities.

“You may have your data in Mombasa; the next time you go to Kisumu, you will be seen by another doctor,” he told more than 600 delegates attending the conference. “If no system can connect the data in Mombasa to Kisumu, then AI is not going to be very useful”, Prof Aluoch explained.

His concerns come as cancer specialists intensify efforts to bring screening and treatment closer to underserved communities. Earlier, Kenya Society of Haematology and Oncology (KESHO), working with Kilifi County and Kilifi County Referral Hospital, conducted an integrated medical outreach offering cervical, breast and prostate cancer screening alongside sickle cell disease testing and specialist consultations.

The programme established referral pathways to Kilifi County Referral Hospital, Moi County Referral Hospital in Voi, Mombasa Cancer Center and Coast General Hospital to support patients requiring further assessment and treatment.

The initiative illustrates one of the challenges facing Kenya’s cancer response: ensuring patients who undergo screening can access diagnosis, specialist treatment and follow-up care without being lost along the referral process.

KESHO Secretary Dr. Anne Mwirigi, a haematologist at Aga Khan University Hospital, and the society’s Treasurer, Dr. Peter Oyiro, a haemato-oncologist at Kenyatta National Hospital, emphasised the importance of effective referrals and continued patient support. Their position reinforces concerns that expanding cancer screening alone will have limited impact unless patients can access timely diagnosis and treatment.

Research cited by KESHO shows the importance of strengthening these services. A 2016 Kenyan study involving 1,094 women attending three breast screening camps found that 14 per cent had abnormal clinical breast examinations, while approximately 1.3 per cent were diagnosed with invasive breast cancer. The findings highlight the need for diagnostic capacity and reliable follow-up arrangements when screening identifies potentially serious conditions.

At the Mombasa conference, Prof. Aluoch said AI could improve the speed and accuracy of cancer diagnosis by helping specialists analyse pathology samples and identify abnormalities that may be difficult to detect through conventional examination. He cited cervical cancer screening as one area where AI-assisted analysis could support earlier detection and reduce the workload on healthcare professionals.

Unlike human specialists, AI systems can process large volumes of diagnostic information without fatigue. However, he cautioned that the technology requires reliable clinical data and cannot compensate for poorly organised health records.
“It’s not like a big computer that you bring from London and sit here,” he said, arguing that Kenyan hospitals must first invest in generating and maintaining accurate digital patient records.
He compared AI to a navigation system that can recommend possible routes but cannot replace the judgement of the person responsible for making the final decision.
The physician maintained that doctors must remain responsible for clinical decisions, even as technology becomes increasingly important in diagnosis and treatment planning.
KESHO President Dr. Gladwell Kiarie also called for stronger government policies and sustainable health financing to ensure advances in cancer care benefit patients beyond major urban hospitals.

She said AI was already helping improve diagnostic processes and multidisciplinary consultations, but warned that patients in rural and marginalised communities continued to face barriers arising from treatment costs and limited specialist services.

The Kilifi outreach was followed by a gynaecological surgical camp, involving Kenyan specialists and partners from Yale and Oxford universities. Kilifi County Director of Health Services Dr. Eddy Nzomo said early diagnosis remained essential to improving treatment outcomes and reaffirmed the county’s commitment to expanding access to cancer services.
For Kenya, the challenge now extends beyond adopting new diagnostic technologies to ensuring that patients can move efficiently from screening to diagnosis, treatment and continued care.
Without reliable patient records, coordinated referrals and adequate specialist services, the benefits of AI-assisted cancer diagnosis may remain beyond the reach of many patients who need them most.

items.title: VetLab’s Aloha Fiesta: Golf, celebration and a captain’s farewell
items.description: VetLab Sports Club held its Aloha Captain's Prize Fiesta 2026 on November 20–21 in Nairobi, as Captain Raj Shah handed over leadership to incoming Captain Eric Mugo.
content: Outgoing Captain Raj Shah hands over to Eric Mugo at VetLab Sports Club’s Aloha Captain’s Prize Fiesta 2026, closing a year of service with laughter, golf, and gratitude.

VetLab Sports Club in Nairobi marked the close of its captaincy year with the Aloha Captain’s Prize Fiesta 2026, a two-day celebration of golf, friendship, and leadership held on Friday and Saturday at the club’s course along Kapenguria Road, Loresho Ridge.

The weekend drew together members, guests, sponsors, and friends of the club for an event that managed to be simultaneously competitive and deeply communal — the kind of gathering that reminds you why golf, at its best, is as much about the people around the course as the shots played on it.

Friday set the tone. Golfers completed their rounds before the evening gave way to a country-themed party that filled the club with music, laughter, and conversation. Members and guests leaned into the theme, and the atmosphere carried the easy warmth of a community that has spent a year building something together.

Saturday brought the golf back to the fore, but the defining moment of the weekend had little to do with scorecards. Outgoing Captain Raj Shah formally handed the captaincy to his Deputy Captain, Eric Mugo, in a ceremony that acknowledged a year of service and signalled the beginning of a new chapter for the club’s leadership.

Shah, who has served as captain for the past year, spoke with characteristic understatement about his time in the role. “I play golf for fun,” he said, with the quiet confidence of someone who has never confused the game’s rewards with its purpose. “The win will come on its own.”

His reflections on the sport itself carried a broader wisdom. “Golf is a game of patience because it really tests your patience,” Shah observed. “The game is growing, with more juniors taking part in it.” It was a remark that pointed beyond the weekend’s celebrations toward something he clearly cares about — the future of the game in Kenya, and the importance of bringing younger players into the fold.

For Mugo, the handover marks the beginning of a captaincy that follows a year spent at close quarters with the role he is now inheriting. The transition carries the advantage of continuity — a deputy who already knows the club’s culture, its members, and the demands of the position is better placed to build on what his predecessor established than to start from scratch.

The Aloha Captain’s Prize Fiesta also served as a moment of institutional recognition for the partners and sponsors who keep club activities possible. Citizen TV and Citizen Digital were among the media partners supporting the celebrations — a reflection of the growing visibility of Kenyan club golf beyond its traditional constituency.

What made the weekend memorable, however, was not the sponsorship or the scoreboards. It was the texture of it — the country outfits on Friday evening, the shared meals, the conversations between rounds, the applause when Shah reflected on his year and the warmth with which Mugo received the captaincy. These are the moments that define a club’s character and determine whether its members return not simply to play golf, but to belong to something.

VetLab Sports Club, tucked along Loresho Ridge in a city that rarely slows down, offered its community exactly that over two days in November. A place to compete, yes — but more importantly, a place to gather, to celebrate, and to pass the torch with the kind of grace that makes an institution worth serving.
As Shah put it, the win comes on its own. What you build in the meantime is what endures.

items.description: Residents of Bamburi in Mombasa County will now enjoy enhanced connectivity following the official launch of the Family Share Plan in the area by Safaricom, in partnership with Huawei. The Family Share
content: Residents of Bamburi in Mombasa County will now enjoy enhanced connectivity following the official launch of the Family Share Plan in the area by Safaricom, in partnership with Huawei.

The Family Share Plan brings together fixed and mobile connectivity under one proposition, enhancing the Home Fibre experience. The solution allows customers to connect up to five family members to a single plan, enabling them to share mobile data and voice minutes while enjoying seamless connectivity both at home and on the go. It also offers families greater convenience, flexibility and value from their Safaricom subscriptions.

Speaking during the rollout event at Zawadi Estate in Bamburi, Mombasa, Fawzia Ali, Chief Consumer Business Officer at Safaricom, said the expansion to the region is part of the company’s nationwide efforts to enhance the Home Fibre experience and deliver greater value to customers.

“The rollout of Family Share in this region is part of our nationwide expansion effort aimed at ensuring that our Home Fibre customers stay connected and enjoy more value from their subscriptions. We have already rolled out the solution in Nairobi and Kisumu, and are now bringing it to Mombasa, with plans to extend it to more parts of the country. Our goal is to ensure families enjoy seamless connectivity and stay connected wherever they are, whether at home or on the go,” said Fawzia.

The Bamburi rollout builds on Safaricom and Huawei’s ongoing collaboration to enhance home connectivity and expand access to integrated digital solutions across the country. It follows the initial rollout in Nairobi and Kisumu, as the two partners continue to extend the Family Share experience to more households across Kenya. Other launch partners include Xiaomi, LG, Ketepa, Farmers Choice, Vision Plus and Unilever.

The plan allows new and existing Safaricom Home Fibre customers to connect up to five family members and share mobile data or voice minutes. By combining Home Fibre with mobile voice, data and SMS benefits, Family Share provides households with a more integrated connectivity experience and the convenience of managing their services through a single bill.

The offering further strengthens Safaricom Home’s customer value proposition, building on recent speed upgrades at no additional cost while bringing fixed and mobile connectivity together. This gives households greater flexibility in managing their communication needs and makes connectivity expenses more predictable.
Starting at KES 3,749, customers can enjoy speeds of 40 Mbps and share either 750 voice minutes or 14GB of mobile data with up to five family members.
Customers can subscribe to Home Fibre or 4G and 5G Wi-Fi plans through My OneApp, by dialling *400#, or by visiting any Safaricom shop or authorised dealer outlet.

content: Kenya’s push to use artificial intelligence in cancer diagnosis could be undermined by fragmented patient records, weak referral systems and unequal access to specialist treatment, medical experts have warned.

content: Konza Technopolis has been designated a Customs Area and allocated a customs code by the Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA), paving the way for faster movement of goods and simplified customs procedures for businesses operating within the smart city.

The designation marks a major step towards making Konza’s Special Economic Zone (SEZ) fully operational, particularly for companies involved in manufacturing, technology development and other businesses that depend on importing and exporting goods.
The development is expected to reduce customs-related delays and improve the ease of doing business, making Konza more attractive to local and international investors.
Technopolis Development Authority Chief Executive Officer John Paul Okwiri said the new status addresses a key requirement for businesses seeking to establish operations within the zone.

“The gazettement of Konza Technopolis as a Customs Area and the allocation of a customs code is a significant step towards making our Special Economic Zone fully operational. It will facilitate the movement of goods, simplify customs processes and create a more enabling environment for investors,” said Okwiri.
Konza Technopolis was gazetted as a Special Economic Zone in July 2019 as part of Kenya’s efforts to attract investment in technology, innovation and industrial development.
The latest approval strengthens the regulatory framework needed to support businesses operating within the smart city and advances Kenya’s ambition to become a knowledge-based economy.

Smartmatic Faces Scrutiny Over Past Election Controversies as Kenya Prepares to Replace KIEMS Kits
items.description: A company whose executives have been criminally charged by the United States Department of Justice (DOJ) over alleged bribery and money laundering schemes has…
content: A company whose executives have been criminally charged by the United States Department of Justice (DOJ) over alleged bribery and money laundering schemes has reportedly received support from prominent political figures as it seeks to remain involved in Kenya’s electoral technology procurement process ahead of the 2027 elections.

In June 2026, the Ministry of Information, Communication and the Digital Economy released a report detailing an independent technical assessment of the Kenya Integrated Elections Management System (KIEMS) kits. The assessment reportedly recommended the decommissioning and replacement of the existing kits with newer technology designed to minimise obsolescence, reduce long-term costs and accommodate emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence.
Following the assessment, the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) initiated a procurement process to replace the tablets supplied by Smartmatic.

Smartmatic has, however, faced legal scrutiny in the United States, where the Department of Justice announced criminal charges against the company and senior executives over allegations of conspiracy to violate the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA) and international money laundering.

According to U.S. prosecutors, the alleged scheme involved approximately $1 million in bribes targeting the former chairman of the Philippine Commission on Elections (COMELEC) in connection with multi-million-dollar electoral technology contracts.

Prosecutors alleged that the scheme involved inflating the prices of voting machines and channeling excess funds through purported consulting arrangements and offshore entities in Asia, Europe and the United States to facilitate payments to corrupt officials.

The company's continued involvement in the Kenyan procurement process has also attracted political debate, with former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua publicly questioning the decision to replace the existing KIEMS technology.

Gachagua reportedly challenged the IEBC's decision to move away from Smartmatic, asking: “Why do we have to remove, to get data from a company that is already in the country and give it a new entrant? What is the gain?”

He also alleged that the proposed transition away from Smartmatic was linked to efforts to manipulate voter registers in particular regions, although the claim was not accompanied by publicly established evidence in the remarks cited.

The debate has raised questions about the influence of political interventions in procurement decisions following the technical assessment recommending the replacement of the existing electoral technology.
Concerns about Smartmatic's track record have also been raised in relation to previous elections in Kenya and other countries.

During the lead-up to Kenya's 2022 elections, three foreign Smartmatic contractors were detained at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport after reportedly carrying sensitive election deployment materials that had not been declared and were allegedly transported without official escorts.

The European Union Election Observation Mission's post-election assessment also highlighted information security weaknesses in the electoral system, including concerns over access controls and the use of shared user accounts that could potentially allow unauthorised access to system functions.

In the Philippines, Smartmatic's electoral technology has faced scrutiny following reported incidents involving corrupted SD cards ahead of the 2019 elections, alleged unauthorised script modifications during vote transmission and a reported security breach involving an employee accused of accepting bribes to facilitate third-party access to secure servers.
The Philippines subsequently barred Smartmatic from participating in its elections, according to reports cited in the allegations against the company.

Other controversies have also been linked to Smartmatic's operations internationally. In El Salvador, reported programming errors involving preferential vote calculations triggered investigations, while in Venezuela, the company's former chief executive publicly alleged that the government had manipulated voter turnout figures by more than one million.
The controversies have renewed scrutiny over the role of electoral technology suppliers, their accountability and the safeguards necessary to protect the integrity of elections.
